newsitem.title: CHINA: HK's H-shares in limelight after 2-1/2 year slump.
newsitem.headline: HK's H-shares in limelight after 2-1/2 year slump.

text.p: Hong Kong-listed mainland Chinese companies have stolen the limelight in the territory's stock market, powered by hopes of a string of earnings-boosting restructurings.
But some market-watchers warn that doubts remain about the fundamentals behind the repackaging.
Analysts cautioned that recent efforts to make H-shares resemble red-chips with asset injection characteristics may not be able to turn around the loss-making Chinese state-owned firms.
Brokers, however, said punters had eagerly welcomed the concept.
"People like the story of the new trend, it's just begun," said Kent Rossiter, a sales manager at Nikko Securities.
H-shares, Hong Kong-listed equity in China-incorporated companies, have been in a two-and-a-half year slump following a string of disappointing corporate earnings.
Red chips, Hong Kong-based companies with Chinese financial backing, have been riding high on hopes of asset injections by their parents. But that all seemed to change last week.
The Hang Seng H-share index hit a 31-month intra-day high of 1,190.45 on Thursday. Even after dipping slightly on Friday on profit taking, it gained 15 percent over the week.
The surge came on the back of hopes that H-share companies will be restructured to boost their future prospects.

"H-shares' earnings are already very bad, their debts are high, and it will not be easy to solve their problems if they do not undergo restructuring," said Ricky Tam, senior research analyst at Delta Asia.
Investors hope reorganisations announced by Shanghai Hai Xing Shipping Co Ltd and Tsingtao Brewery Co Ltd earlier this month will be the start of a trend.
Lawrence Ang, head of China Research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said the success of Hai Xing's restructuring was evidence of Beijing's will to reactivate the H-share market.
"The Hai Xing restructuring, which was a complicated task and a breakthrough for H-shares, could not possibly be achieved if without central government's endorsement," Ang said.

Hai Xing had said its Shanghai-based parent would transfer control to China Shipping (Group) Co, a national conglomerate under the auspices of the State Council, or cabinet, formed by the merger of several large mainland shipping companies.
Hai Xing shares ended Friday at HK$5.50, up 28.65 percent since July 11 when the shift of parents was announced.

Shares of Tsingtao Brewery also jumped 53.85 percent this past week to close Friday at HK$5.00 on news that the brewery was undergoing a restructuring aimed at rebuilding its stock market image and boosting earnings.
However, analysts warned China-based H-share companies were under more rigid Chinese regulation and were less flexible when compared with Hong Kong-based red chip companies.

"We believe the chance (for restructurings) is not so prominent for the large cap H-shares since a huge amount of assets will be needed to enhance earnings of these companies," said Percy Au-Young, research director at DBS Securities.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell estimated average earnings per share growth for H-shares in calendar 1997 to be eight percent.
"But we probably will have to revise down the forecast after the interim result announcements," Ang said.

Andrew To, dealing director at OSK Securities, also said restructuring was not an easy task as many of the H-shares were single-industry companies, and injections would likely be confined to industry-related assets.
"This will not help earnings if the industry itself is problematic, such as petrochemical and iron and steel industries which face over-supply and keen competition," he said.
What would benefit H-shares directly was for Beijing to reform China's state-owned industry sector, Au-Young said.

"Since most H-share companies and their customers are state-owned and if state enterprises can be turned around, it will boost product demand and solve the triangular (gridlocked) debt problem, and that will help," he said.
